newsitem.title: UK: Precious outlook - PGMs to set tone for complex.
newsitem.headline: Precious outlook - PGMs to set tone for complex.

text.p: Currency gyrations and potential fireworks in the platinum group metals (PGMs) will help set the tone for the precious metals this week, dealers said, but closed U.K. and U.S. markets on Monday will make for a slow start.
Platinum and palladium soared early last week -- palladium fixed at 6-1/2 year highs on Tuesday -- as growing anxiety about delayed Russian supplies escalated.
But they retraced their steps on fresh news that long-delayed talks between Russian suppliers and Japanese buyers are due to begin next month.
As new details emerge, more speculative and investor selling could be sparked, which could touch the entire precious complex, dealers said.
"Platinum and palladium remain the main factors in the precious complex," a trader said.
"Sentiment doesn't look good and the PGMS have been putting gold under pressure."
Currency movements, particularly dollar/yen, could be equally important in carving out the near term direction of the market, dealers added.
A weakening yen last Friday helped speed palladium's slump by encouraging investors to get rid of their yen-based palladium futures.
"We've seen the yen between 112 and 119 against the dollar recently and that's not helped stabilise the precious metals," a dealer said.
Platinum ended the week at $389.00/$390.00, after approaching $400 at the week's highs, while palladium settled at $172.50/$173.50, versus a high of $181.50.
Gold has been shadowing the PGMs to some degree, but it failed to budge from a $340-$345 price range last week in sluggish trading. It settled at $342.80/$343.30 on Friday in London.
But given the right conditions, a break to the downside below key $339.70 support, could trigger further losses to the year's low around $336, analysts said.
Continued weakening of the Australian dollar against the U.S. dollar could convince Australian producers to start selling metal and send spot gold prices spiralling.
"For the most part they're still waiting for that little bit higher price," a dealer said.
"But if it gold hits $450 Australian dollars and ounce, it'll probably be enough for the producers to start selling.
Silver, which closed at $4.74/$4.76 on Friday afternoon, was expected to follow the other metals' lead.
The market had been mostly range-bound last week until a flurry of speculative buying lifted it by nearly 15 cents on Friday afternoon, boosting the other precious metals.
